newsitem.title: INDIA: India Congress party leadership race hots up.
newsitem.headline: India Congress party leadership race hots up.

text.p: Former defence minister Sharad Pawar entered the leadership race of India's Congress party on Wednesday, intensifying a power struggle in the country's oldest political machine.

"The Congress is fighting for its existence. There is a crisis of both leadership and credibility," Pawar told a news conference after filing his nomination to challenge the party's current president, Sitaram Kesri.
Pawar was preceded by another would-be Congress leader, former junior Home Minister Rajesh Pilot, who filed his papers on Tuesday to run in the leadership vote to be held on June 9.
Their moves signalled a major thrust against Kesri, a veteran seen by critics as incapable of reviving a party that suffered its worst humiliation in elections last year.
"If Kesri stays, we can't win the next election," said former Textiles Minister G. Venkatswamy, a Pawar supporter.
The Congress party, which has ruled India for all but five years since independence from Britain in 1947, has not had a contest for its top post since 1977.

For two decades, it has practised a culture of unanimity, mostly under the towering presence of the Nehru-Gandhi political family, three of whose members have ruled as prime ministers for a total of 38 years.

Pawar said he expected to work out an arrangement with the other contestant, Pilot, to ensure a direct contest with Kesri. Kesri was expected to file his papers later on Wednesday, the deadline for nominations.
Although the Congress party is out of power, it wields influence through its support for Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's centre-left United Front coalition.
Kesri's popularity plunged in March when he withdrew support from the then United Front prime minister, H.D. Deve Gowda. He resumed support for the coalition after it changed its leader.
Kesri's whimsical style and his age, 77, are seen as handicaps by Congress leaders.
Party leaders say the vacuum created by the assassination of former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi in 1991 remains unfilled.
Lower castes and minority Moslem voters, traditional Congress supporters, have steadily moved away from the party. Senior leaders have been tainted by corruption scandals.
Sonia Gandhi, Rajiv's Italian-born widow, enrolled as a Congress member a few weeks ago but she has not accepted demands from party officials that she take up the leadership.
"We can save the Congress if Sonia Gandhi comes. But since she did not, there was no alternative but to contest (Kesri)," Venkatswamy said.
Kesri took charge of the party from former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, who resigned last September after a court brought charges against him in a cheating case in which he denies wrongdoing.
The new president will be chosen by about 8,000 party delegates, with the result expected on June 12.
